subject: n_divergent=1 in sampling even after adapt_delta=0.99

messages.author: 007eb1d250836bea
messages.subject: n_divergent=1 in sampling even after adapt_delta=0.99
parts:
Hello all,

Sorry to bombard mail boxes of late.

I have had a look at my own meta-analysis models, (aside from the BUGS examples that I am translating), and have found for one of them, that n_divergent=1 even after I have changed adapt_delta=0.99. 

I also find that when I increase the delta parameter from its default of 0.8 to 0.99, that the tree_depth sometimes hits the maximum, and the n_leapfrog also sometimes exceeds its max of 1000.

I include the model below, it seems than when I move from a sampling scheme to a negative binomial, I get this problem. (It does not occur with the poisson scheme to be clear).

Best,

Ben

data {

  ## Single release parameters
  int<lower=0> N; ## Total number of observations
  int<lower=0> K; ## Total number of groups
  int Y[N]; ## Vector of observations for the release
  int S[K]; ## Array of ints for the group sizes
  vector[N] t; ## Vector of time observations (days) 
  int Pos[K]; ## Array of the starting position of each dataset
  
  ## Multiple release parameters
  int RelFreq[K]; ## Array of the frequency of releases in each study
  int PosRel[K]; ## Array of the starting position of releases in each study in RelNumber vector
  int<lower=0> NReleases; ## Total number of releases across all studies
  vector[NReleases] RelNumber; ## Vector of the numbers released across each study
  vector[NReleases] RelTime; ## Release time of each release in each study. For the majority of these studies, this will be simply be '0' corresponding to single release
} 


parameters {
  real mPsi;
  real<lower=0> sigmaPsi;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> psi[K];
  real mMu;
  real<lower=0> sigmaMu;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> mu[K];
  real<lower=0> kappa[K];
  real<lower=0.1> p;
  real<lower=0.1> r;
  
  ## Convenient parameters
  real overallLogitMu;
  real overallLogitPsi;
  real overallKappa;
} 

  
transformed parameters {
  real overallMu;
  real overallPsi;
  real lifeExpectancy;
  real phi[K];
  real eta[K];
  overallMu <- inv_logit(overallLogitMu);
  overallPsi <- inv_logit(overallLogitPsi);
  lifeExpectancy <- (1/overallMu) - 1;
  for (i in 1:K)
  {
phi[i] <- logit(psi[i]);
eta[i] <- logit(mu[i]);
  }
}
 
model {
  for (i in 1:K) {
real lambda[S[i]];
if (RelFreq[i]< 2) ## Single release
{
real R_times_psi;
R_times_psi <- RelNumber[PosRel[i]]*psi[i];
for (j in 1:S[i])
{
lambda[j]<- R_times_psi*(1 - mu[i])^t[Pos[i] + j - 1];
Y[Pos[i] + j - 1] ~ neg_binomial_2(lambda[j],kappa[i]);
}
}
else ## Multiple release
{
for (j in 1:S[i])
{
real lambdaTemp;
lambdaTemp <- 0;
for (kk in 1:RelFreq[i])
{
if (t[Pos[i] + j - 1]> RelTime[PosRel[i]+kk-1])
{
lambdaTemp <- lambdaTemp + psi[i]*RelNumber[PosRel[i] + kk - 1]*(1-mu[i])^(t[Pos[i] + j - 1] - RelTime[PosRel[i]+kk-1]);
}
}
lambda[j] <- lambdaTemp;
Y[Pos[i] + j - 1] ~ neg_binomial_2(lambda[j],kappa[i]);
}
}
  }
  ## Basic
  eta ~ normal(mMu,sigmaMu);
  phi ~ normal(mPsi,sigmaPsi);
  mMu ~ normal(0,100);
  mPsi ~ normal(0,100);
  sigmaMu ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  sigmaPsi ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  
  ## Negative binomial
  kappa ~ gamma(p,r);
  p ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  r ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  
  ## Convenient parameters
  overallLogitMu ~ normal(mMu,sigmaMu); ## Overall mu
  overallLogitPsi ~ normal(mPsi,sigmaPsi); ## Overall Psi
  overallKappa ~ gamma(p,r);
}

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] n_divergent=1 in sampling even after adapt_delta=0.99
parts: > I also find that when I increase the delta parameter from its default of 0.8 to 0.99, that the tree_depth sometimes hits the maximum, and the n_leapfrog also sometimes exceeds its max of 1000.

This is expected — the smaller the step size the more leapfrog steps you need to
achieve the same integration time. Because Hamiltonian trajectories can meander
off for infinite time in non-identifiable models we have a hard maximum in the
depth of the NUTS tree (and hence number of leapfrog steps). It’s set to 10 by
default, hence the 2^10 = 1024 steps that you’re seeing.

All you have to do is increase the max_depth argument and rerun.

> ## Basic
> eta ~ normal(mMu,sigmaMu);
> phi ~ normal(mPsi,sigmaPsi);
> mMu ~ normal(0,100);
> mPsi ~ normal(0,100);
> sigmaMu ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
> sigmaPsi ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

There’s your problem! You’re using a centered hierarchical parameterization
for the eta and phi. Switch this to a non-centered parameterization (see the
manual if you’re not sure how to do this) and the divergences should go away.

I’d also reconsider those normal(0, 100) priors — 100 is a pretty extreme
value.

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Re: n_divergent=1 in sampling even after adapt_delta=0.99
parts:
Hi,

I think I can answer my own question, so I'll post it here. I was having an issue because kappa varies considerably in scale according to whether poisson sampling (kappa->inf) was appropriate vs negative_binomial (if kappa is of order 20 or less). I think because of this extreme scale change, the integrator was diverging at a lot of iterations, and hence missing areas of high curvature. (Someone correct me if I am wrong).

However, a re-parameterisation by placing a normal prior on log(kappa), seemed to prevent the integrator from diverging.

Best,

Ben

messages.author: 89abf8a3796a510b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: n_divergent=1 in sampling even after adapt_delta=0.99
parts:
Ben,

FYI, in your code above, you have a normal prior on a transformed parameter without adding the log-jacobian of the transformation to the log density. That would also be problematic for your model.

You need to put phi and eta in your parameters block and make psi and mu transformed parameters with
for (i in 1:K) {

psi[i] <- inv_logit(phi[i]);
  mu[i] <- inv_logit(eta[i]);
}

Also, having convenient parameters overallLogitMu, overallLogitPsi, overallKappa in your parameters block rather than in a generated quantities block will slow your model down given that Stan is taking partial derivatives of these parameters when it doesn't need to.

So something like:

generated quantities {
  real overallLogitMu;

  overallLogitMu <- normal_rng(mMu, sigmaMu);
}


Rob

parts:
Priors can definitely help stop the sampler running away.

You should also check out the non-centered parameterizations,
which could also make things more efficient. And they're what
we're going to want to make standard operating procedure for our
recoding of the BUGS and ARM models.

- Bob

parts:
Hi Mike,

Thanks for your message.

I have tried the following reparameterisation (which I took from the manual). It does not seem to make things any faster, and seems to get stuck forever in warmup.

I illustrate it here just for the parameter 'eta', although it applied to 'phi' as well.

parameters {
...
real<lower=0,upper=1> mu[K]; ## parameters of interest
real etaRaw[K];

real mMu;
real<lower=0> sigmaMu;
}

transformed parameters {
...
real eta[K];

for (i in 1:K)
{

eta[i] <- logit(mu[i]); ## mu is the parameter of interest
    eta[i] <- mMu + sigmaMu*etaRaw[i];    
}

}

model {
    ...
    etaRaw ~ normal(0,1);
    mMu ~ normal(0,5); 
    sigmaMu ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
}

Is this the non-centralisation/'Matt trick' that you had in mind?

Best,

Ben

> I also find that when I increase the delta parameter from its default of 0.8 to 0.99, that the tree_depth sometimes hits the maximum, and the n_leapfrog also sometimes exceeds its max of 1000.

achieve the same integration time.  Because Hamiltonian trajectories can meander
off for infinite time in non-identifiable models we have a hard maximum in the
depth of the NUTS tree (and hence number of leapfrog steps).  It’s set to 10 by
default, hence the 2^10 = 1024 steps that you’re seeing.

All you have to do is increase the max_depth argument and rerun.

>   ## Basic
>   eta ~ normal(mMu,sigmaMu);
>   phi ~ normal(mPsi,sigmaPsi);
>   mMu ~ normal(0,100);
>   mPsi ~ normal(0,100);
>   sigmaMu ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>   sigmaPsi ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

There’s your problem!  You’re using a centered hierarchical parameterization
for the eta and phi.  Switch this to a non-centered parameterization (see the

I’d also reconsider those normal(0, 100) priors — 100 is a pretty extreme
value.

On May 13, 2015, at 1:15 PM, Ben Lambert <ben.c....@googlemail.com> wrote:

Hi Mike,

Thanks for your message.

I have tried the following reparameterisation (which I took from the manual). It does not seem to make things any faster, and seems to get stuck forever in warmup.

I illustrate it here just for the parameter 'eta', although it applied to 'phi' as well.

parameters {
...
real<lower=0,upper=1> mu[K]; ## parameters of interest
real etaRaw[K];
real mMu;
real<lower=0> sigmaMu;
}

transformed parameters {
...
real eta[K];

for (i in 1:K)
{
    eta[i] <- logit(mu[i]); ## mu is the parameter of interest
    eta[i] <- mMu + sigmaMu*etaRaw[i];    
}

}

model {
    ...
    etaRaw ~ normal(0,1);
    mMu ~ normal(0,5); 
    sigmaMu ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
}

Is this the non-centralisation/'Matt trick' that you had in mind?

Best,

Ben

On Tuesday, May 12, 2015 at 6:34:11 PM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> I also find that when I increase the delta parameter from its default of 0.8 to 0.99, that the tree_depth sometimes hits the maximum, and the n_leapfrog also sometimes exceeds its max of 1000.

This is expected — the smaller the step size the more leapfrog steps you need to
achieve the same integration time.  Because Hamiltonian trajectories can meander
off for infinite time in non-identifiable models we have a hard maximum in the
depth of the NUTS tree (and hence number of leapfrog steps).  It’s set to 10 by
default, hence the 2^10 = 1024 steps that you’re seeing.

All you have to do is increase the max_depth argument and rerun.

>   ## Basic
>   eta ~ normal(mMu,sigmaMu);
>   phi ~ normal(mPsi,sigmaPsi);
>   mMu ~ normal(0,100);
>   mPsi ~ normal(0,100);
>   sigmaMu ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>   sigmaPsi ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

There’s your problem!  You’re using a centered hierarchical parameterization
for the eta and phi.  Switch this to a non-centered parameterization (see the
manual if you’re not sure how to do this) and the divergences should go away.

I’d also reconsider those normal(0, 100) priors — 100 is a pretty extreme
value.
--
